also provide a source of nutrients for <color=#3366CC>scavengers</color>, <color=#3366CC>detrivores</color> and <color=#3366CC>riparian</color> florae, making trout <color=#3366CC>keystone species</color> across
<color=#3366CC>aquatic</color> and terrestrial ecosystems.

Anatomy
Trout that live in different environments can have dramatically different colorations and patterns. Mostly, these colors
and patterns form as <color=#3366CC>camouflage</color>, based on the surroundings, and will change as the fish moves to different habitats.
Trout in, or newly returned from the sea, can look very silvery, while the same fish living in a small stream or in an
alpine lake could have pronounced markings and more vivid coloration; it is also possible that in some species, this
signifies that they are ready to mate. In general, trout that are about to breed have extremely intense coloration and can
look like an entirely different fish outside of spawning season. It is virtually impossible to define a particular color pattern
as belonging to a specific breed; however, in general, wild fish are claimed to have more vivid colors and patterns.
Trout have fins entirely without spines, and all of them have a small <color=#3366CC>adipose</color> fin along the back, near the tail. The pelvic
fins sit well back on the body, on each side of the anus. The swim bladder is connected to the <color=#3366CC>esophagus</color>, allowing for
gulping or rapid expulsion of air, a condition known as physostome. Unlike many other physostome fish, trout do not
use their bladder as an auxiliary device for <color=#3366CC>oxygen</color> uptake, relying solely on their <color=#3366CC>gills</color>.
There are many species, and even more populations, that are isolated from each other and morphologically different.
However, since many of these distinct populations show no significant genetic differences, what may appear to be a
large number of species is considered a much smaller number of distinct species by most <color=#3366CC>ichthyologists</color>. The trout
found in the eastern <color=#3366CC>United States</color> are a good example of this. The brook trout, the aurora trout, and the (extinct) silver
trout all have physical characteristics and colorations that distinguish them, yet <color=#3366CC>genetic</color> analysis shows that they are
one species, Salvelinus fontinalis.
Lake trout (Salvelinus namaycush), like brook trout, belong to the char genus. Lake trout inhabit many of the larger
lakes in North America, and live much longer than <color=#3366CC>rainbow trout</color>, which have an average maximum lifespan of seven
years. Lake trout can live many decades, and can grow to more than 30 kg.
Habitat
As salmonids, trout are <color=#3366CC>coldwater fish</color> that are usually found in cool (50 – 60 F), clear streams, wetlands and lakes,
although many of the species have <color=#3366CC>anadromous</color> populations as well. Juvenile trout are referred to as troutlet, troutling
or parr. They are distributed naturally throughout <color=#3366CC>North America</color>, northern <color=#3366CC>Asia</color> and <color=#3366CC>Europe</color>. Several species of trout
were introduced to <color=#3366CC>Australia</color> and <color=#3366CC>New Zealand</color> by amateur fishing enthusiasts in the 19th century, effectively displacing
and endangering several <color=#3366CC>upland</color> native fish species. The introduced species included brown trout from <color=#3366CC>England</color> and
<color=#3366CC>rainbow trout</color> from <color=#3366CC>California</color>. The rainbow trout has a steelhead subspecies, generally accepted as coming from
Sonoma Creek. The rainbow trout of New Zealand still show the steelhead tendency to run up rivers in winter to spawn.
In Australia, the rainbow trout was introduced in 1894 from New Zealand and is an extremely popular gamefish in
recreational angling. Despite severely impacting the distribution and abundance of native Australian fish, such as the
climbing galaxias, millions of rainbow and other trout species are released annually from government and private
hatcheries.
The closest resemblance of seema trout and other trout family can be found in the <color=#3366CC>Himalayan Region</color> of India, Nepal,
Bhutan, Pakistan and in <color=#3366CC>Tian Shan</color> mountains of <color=#3366CC>Kyrgyzstan</color>.
Diet

Trout generally feed on other fish, and soft-bodied aquatic <color=#3366CC>invertebrates</color>, such as <color=#3366CC>flies</color>, <color=#3366CC>mayflies</color>, <color=#3366CC>caddisflies</color>, <color=#3366CC>stoneflies</color>,
<color=#3366CC>mollusks</color> and <color=#3366CC>dragonflies</color>. In lakes, various species of <color=#3366CC>zooplankton</color> often form a large part of the diet. In general, trout
longer than about 300 mm prey almost exclusively on fish, where they are available. Adult trout will devour smaller fish
up to one-third of their length. Trout may feed on <color=#3366CC>shrimp</color>, mealworms, bloodworms, <color=#3366CC>insects</color>, small animal parts, and <color=#3366CC>eel</color>.
Trout who swim the streams love to feed on land animals, aquatic life, and flies. Most of their diet comes from
macroinvertebrates, or animals that do not have a backbone like snails, worms, or insects. They also eat flies, and
most people who try to use lures to fish trout mimic flies because they are one of trout's most fed on meals. Trout enjoy
certain land animals, including insects like grasshoppers. They also eat small animals like mice when they fall in.
(Although only large trout have mouths capable of eating mice.) They consume a diet of aquatic life like minnows or
crawfish as well. Trout have a diverse diet they follow; they have plenty of different options.
Trout as food
Compared to other salmonids, trout are somewhat more bony, but the flesh is generally considered delicious, and the
texture is often indistinguishable from <color=#3366CC>that of salmon</color>. The flavor of the flesh is heavily influenced by the diet of the fish.
For example, trout that have been feeding on crustaceans tend to be more flavorful than those feeding primarily on
<color=#3366CC>insects</color> and <color=#3366CC>larvae</color>. Because of their popularity, trout are often raised on <color=#3366CC>fish farms</color> and then stocked into heavily fished
waters, in an effort to mask the effects of <color=#3366CC>overfishing</color>. Farmed trout are also sold commercially as <color=#3366CC>seafood</color>, although
they are not <color=#3366CC>saltwater fish</color>. Trout meat is typically prepared the same way as salmon, often by <color=#3366CC>smoking</color>.
In Mainland China, farm-raised <color=#3366CC>rainbow trout</color> from <color=#3366CC>Qinghai</color> was officially sanctioned to be labeled and sold domestically
as salmon, which caused controversy in 2018 regarding <color=#3366CC>food safety</color> and consumer rights violation, as raw fish dishes or
yusheng using <color=#3366CC>Atlantic salmon</color> are gaining popularity in southern China. Farmed rainbow trout is much cheaper than
the imported Atlantic salmon and the meat are indistinguishable to the untrained eyes, and the news of trout being sold
as salmon triggered public scrutiny accusing seafood suppliers of bait-and-switch and unethical business practices.
Also, many people believe freshwater trout are more prone to parasites than oceanic salmon (even though both live in
freshwater for significant periods of their life cycles) and thus unsafe for raw eating.

Trout fishing
Trout are very popular freshwater game fish highly prized especially by creek fishermen, because they generally put up
a good fight when caught with a <color=#3366CC>hook</color> and <color=#3366CC>line</color>. As trout are predatory fish, <color=#3366CC>lure fishing</color> (which use replica baits called
<color=#3366CC>lures</color> to imitate live prey) is the predominant form of <color=#3366CC>sport fishing</color> involving trout, although traditional bait fishing
techniques using <color=#3366CC>floats</color> and/or sinkers (particularly with moving live baits such as baitfish, <color=#3366CC>crayfish</color> or aquatic insects)
are also successful, especially against stocked trout that are <color=#3366CC>hatchery</color>/<color=#3366CC>farm</color>-raised and thus more accustomed to
artificial feeds.
Many species of trout, most noticeably <color=#3366CC>rainbow trout</color> and brown trout, have been widely introduced into waterbodies
outside of their native ranges purely for the sake of <color=#3366CC>recreational fishing</color>, and some of these introduced populations have
even become <color=#3366CC>invasive</color> in the new habitats.
River fishing
While trout can be caught with a normal <color=#3366CC>rod</color> and <color=#3366CC>reel</color>, <color=#3366CC>fly fishing</color> is a distinctive lure fishing method developed for trout,
and now extended to other species. Due to the high proportion of <color=#3366CC>insects</color> and small <color=#3366CC>crustaceans</color> within the trout's diet,
small lures made of hand-tied <color=#3366CC>hairs</color> and <color=#3366CC>threads</color> are often used to imitate these aquatic <color=#3366CC>invertebrates</color> that the trout prey
upon. These ultralight fly lures cannot be <color=#3366CC>cast</color> adequately by conventional techniques, and a specialized heavy line (i.e.
fly line) is needed to launch the lure.
Understanding how moving water shapes the stream channel makes it easier to find trout. In most streams, the current
creates a riffle-run-pool pattern that repeats itself over and over. A deep pool may hold a big brown trout, but rainbow
trout and smaller brown trout are likely found in runs. Riffles are where fishers will find small trout, called troutlet, during
the day and larger trout crowding in during morning and evening feeding periods.
• Riffles have a fast current and shallow water. This gives way to a bottom of gravel, rubble or boulder. Riffles are
morning and evening feeding areas. Trout usually spawn just above or below riffles, but may spawn right in them.
• Runs are deeper than riffles with a moderate current and are found between riffles and pools. The bottom is made
up of small gravel or rubble. These hot spots hold trout almost anytime, if there is sufficient cover.
• Pools are smoother and look darker than the other areas of the stream. The deep, slow-moving water generally
has a bottom of silt, sand, or small gravel. Pools make good midday resting spots for medium to large trout.
• It is recommended that when fishing for trout, that the fisher(s) should use line in the 4–8 lb test for streamfish, and
stronger line with the same diameter for trout from the sea or from a large lake, such as Lake Michigan. It is also
recommended to use a hook size 8–5 for trout of all kind. Trout, especially farm-raised ones, tend to like salmon
roes, <color=#3366CC>worms</color>, <color=#3366CC>minnows</color>, cut bait, <color=#3366CC>maize</color>, or marshmallows.
Ice fishing
Fishing for trout under the ice generally occurs in depths of 4 to 8 ft. Because trout are cold water fish, during the winter
they move from up-deep to the shallows, replacing the small fish that inhabit the area during the summer. Trout in
winter constantly cruise in shallow depths looking for food, usually traveling in groups, although bigger fish may travel
alone and in water that's somewhat deeper, around 12 ft. Rainbow, Brown, and Brook trout are the most common trout
species caught through the ice.

Declines in native trout populations
Salmonid populations in general have been declining due to numerous factors, including <color=#3366CC>invasive species</color>,
hybridization, wildfires, and climate change. Native salmonid fish in the western and southwestern United States are
threatened by non-native species that were introduced decades ago. Non-native salmonids were introduced to enrich
recreational fishing; however, they quickly started outcompeting and displacing native salmonids upon their arrival.
Non-native, invasive species are quick to adapt to their new environment and learn to outcompete any native species,
making them a force the native salmon and trout have to reckon with. Not only do the non-native fish drive the native
fish to occupy new niches, but they also try to hybridize with them, contaminating the native gene construction. As more
hybrids between native and non-native fish are formed, the lineage of the pure fish is continuously being contaminated
by other species and soon may no longer represent the sole native species. The Rio Grande cutthroat trout
(Oncorhynchus clarki virginalis) are susceptible to hybridization with other salmonids such as <color=#3366CC>rainbow trout</color>
(Oncorhynchus mykiss) and yield a new "cutbow" trout, which is a contamination of both lineages' genes. One solution
to this issue is implemented by New Mexico Department of Game and Fish <color=#3366CC>hatcheries</color>: stock only sterile fish in river
streams. Hatcheries serve as a reservoir of fish for recreational activities but growing and stocking non-sterile fish
would worsen the hybridization issue on a quicker, more magnified time scale. By stocking sterile fish, the native
salmonids can't share genes with the non-native hatchery fish, thus, preventing further gene contamination of the native
trout in New Mexico. Fire is also a factor in deteriorating Gila trout (Oncorhynchus gilae) populations because of the
ash and soot that can enter streams following fires. The ash lowers water quality, making it more difficult for the Gila
trout to survive. In some New Mexico streams, the native Gila trout will be evacuated from streams that are threatened
by nearby fires and be reintroduced after the threat is resolved.
<color=#3366CC>Climate change</color> is also dwindling native salmonid populations. <color=#3366CC>Global warming</color> continually affects various cold-water
fish such as trout, especially as inland waterbodies are more prone to warming than oceans. With an increase of
temperature along with changes in spawning river flow, an abundance of trout species are affected negatively. In the
past, a mere 8 F-change increase was predicted to eliminate half of the native brook trout in the Southern <color=#3366CC>Appalachian</color>
<color=#3366CC>Mountains</color>. Trout generally prefer streams with colder water (50 – 60 F) to spawn and thrive, but raising water
temperatures are altering this ecosystem and further deteriorate native populations.
Arabic script
The Arabic script is the <color=#3366CC>writing system</color> used for <color=#3366CC>Arabic</color> (<color=#3366CC>Arabic alphabet</color>) and several other languages of Asia and
Africa. It is the second-most widely used <color=#3366CC>alphabetic</color> writing system in the world (after the <color=#3366CC>Latin script</color>), the second-most
widely used writing system in the world by number of countries using it, and the third-most by number of users (after
the Latin and <color=#3366CC>Chinese scripts</color>).
The script was first used to write texts in Arabic, most notably the <color=#3366CC>Quran</color>, the holy book of <color=#3366CC>Islam</color>. With the religion's
spread, it came to be used as the primary script for many language families, leading to the addition of new letters and

other symbols. Such languages using it are <color=#3366CC>Arabic</color>, <color=#3366CC>Persian</color> (Farsi and <color=#3366CC>Dari</color>), <color=#3366CC>Urdu</color>, <color=#3366CC>Uyghur</color>, <color=#3366CC>Kurdish</color>, <color=#3366CC>Pashto</color>, <color=#3366CC>Punjabi</color>

(Shahmukhi), <color=#3366CC>Sindhi</color>, Saraiki, <color=#3366CC>Azerbaijani</color> (Torki in <color=#3366CC>Iran</color>), <color=#3366CC>Malay</color> (<color=#3366CC>Jawi</color>), <color=#3366CC>Javanese</color>, <color=#3366CC>Sundanese</color>, <color=#3366CC>Madurese</color> and
<color=#3366CC>Indonesian</color> (Pegon), Balti, Balochi, Hindko, Luri, <color=#3366CC>Kashmiri</color>, Cham (Akhar Srak), Rohingya, <color=#3366CC>Somali</color>, Mandinka, and
<color=#3366CC>Mooré</color>, among others. Until the 16th century, it was also used for some Spanish texts, and—prior to the script reform in
1928—it was the writing system of <color=#3366CC>Turkish</color>.
The script is written from <color=#3366CC>right to left</color> in a <color=#3366CC>cursive</color> style, in which most of the letters are written in slightly different forms
according to whether they stand alone or are joined to a following or preceding letter. The script is unicase and does
not have distinct capital or lowercase letters. In most cases, the letters transcribe <color=#3366CC>consonants</color>, or consonants and a few
vowels, so most Arabic alphabets are <color=#3366CC>abjads</color>, with the versions used for some languages, such as Sorani dialect of
Kurdish, <color=#3366CC>Kashmiri</color>, Gorani, Uyghur and Serbo-Croatian being <color=#3366CC>alphabets</color>, while Mandarin having an <color=#3366CC>abugida</color> where
diacritics are showed instead of full letters. It is the basis for the tradition of Arabic calligraphy.
History
The Arabic alphabet is derived either from the Nabataean alphabet or (less widely believed) directly from the Syriac
alphabet, which are both derived from the Aramaic alphabet, which, in turn, descended from the <color=#3366CC>Phoenician alphabet</color>.
The Phoenician script also gave rise to the <color=#3366CC>Greek alphabet</color> (and, therefore, both the <color=#3366CC>Cyrillic alphabet</color> and the <color=#3366CC>Latin</color>
<color=#3366CC>alphabet</color> used in North and South America and most European countries).
Origins
In the 6th and 5th centuries BCE, northern Arab tribes emigrated and founded a kingdom centred around <color=#3366CC>Petra</color>,
Jordan. This people (now named Nabataeans from the name of one of the tribes, Nabatu) spoke Nabataean Arabic, a
dialect of the <color=#3366CC>Arabic</color> language. In the 2nd or 1st centuries BCE, the first known records of the Nabataean alphabet were
written in the <color=#3366CC>Aramaic language</color> (which was the language of communication and trade), but included some Arabic
language features: the Nabataeans did not write the language which they spoke. They wrote in a form of the Aramaic
alphabet, which continued to evolve; it separated into two forms: one intended for <color=#3366CC>inscriptions</color> (known as "monumental
Nabataean") and the other, more cursive and hurriedly written and with joined letters, for writing on <color=#3366CC>papyrus</color>. This
cursive form influenced the monumental form more and more and gradually changed into the Arabic alphabet.
Overview
The Arabic script has been adapted for use in a wide variety of languages aside from Arabic, including <color=#3366CC>Persian</color>, <color=#3366CC>Malay</color>
and <color=#3366CC>Urdu</color>, which are not <color=#3366CC>Semitic</color>. Such adaptations may feature altered or new characters to represent <color=#3366CC>phonemes</color> that
do not appear in Arabic <color=#3366CC>phonology</color>. For example, the Arabic language lacks a voiceless bilabial plosive (the sound),
therefore many languages add their own letter to represent in the script, though the specific letter used varies from
language to language. These modifications tend to fall into groups: Indian and <color=#3366CC>Turkic languages</color> written in the Arabic
script tend to use the <color=#3366CC>Persian modified letters</color>, whereas the languages of Indonesia tend to imitate those of <color=#3366CC>Jawi</color>. The
modified version of the Arabic script originally devised for use with Persian is known as the <color=#3366CC>Perso-Arabic script</color> by
scholars.

When the Arabic script is used to write <color=#3366CC>Serbo-Croatian</color>, <color=#3366CC>Sorani</color>, <color=#3366CC>Kashmiri</color>, <color=#3366CC>Mandarin Chinese</color>, or <color=#3366CC>Uyghur</color>, vowels are
mandatory. The Arabic script can, therefore, be used as a true <color=#3366CC>alphabet</color> as well as an <color=#3366CC>abjad</color>, although it is often
strongly, if erroneously, connected to the latter due to it being originally used only for Arabic.
Use of the Arabic script in <color=#3366CC>West African</color> languages, especially in the <color=#3366CC>Sahel</color>, developed with the spread of <color=#3366CC>Islam</color>. To a
certain degree the style and usage tends to follow those of the <color=#3366CC>Maghreb</color> (for instance the position of the dots in the
letters fā and qāf). Additional <color=#3366CC>diacritics</color> have come into use to facilitate the writing of sounds not represented in the
Arabic language. The term Ajamī, which comes from the Arabic root for "foreign", has been applied to Arabic-based
orthographies of African languages.

Former use
With the establishment of Muslim rule in the <color=#3366CC>subcontinent</color>, one or more forms of the Arabic script were incorporated
among the assortment of scripts used for writing native languages. In the 20th century, the Arabic script was generally

replaced by the <color=#3366CC>Latin alphabet</color> in the <color=#3366CC>Balkans</color>, parts of <color=#3366CC>Sub-Saharan Africa</color>, and <color=#3366CC>Southeast Asia</color>, while in the <color=#3366CC>Soviet</color>
<color=#3366CC>Union</color>, after a brief period of Latinisation, use of <color=#3366CC>Cyrillic</color> was mandated. <color=#3366CC>Turkey</color> changed to the Latin alphabet in 1928
as part of an internal Westernizing revolution. After the collapse of the Soviet Union in 1991, many of the Turkic
languages of the ex-USSR attempted to follow Turkey's lead and convert to a Turkish-style Latin alphabet. However,
renewed use of the Arabic alphabet has occurred to a limited extent in <color=#3366CC>Tajikistan</color>, whose language's close resemblance
to <color=#3366CC>Persian</color> allows direct use of publications from Afghanistan and Iran.

Letter construction
Most languages that use alphabets based on the Arabic alphabet use the same base shapes. Most additional letters in
languages that use alphabets based on the Arabic alphabet are built by adding (or removing) diacritics to existing
Arabic letters. Some stylistic variants in Arabic have distinct meanings in other languages. For example, variant forms
of kāf are used in some languages and sometimes have specific usages. In Urdu and some neighbouring languages,
the letter Hā has diverged into two forms dō-čašmī hē and gōl hē, while a variant form of yā referred to as barī yē is
used at the end of some words.
